title: Field Assist
pitch: Field Assist lets Codex and a human expert turn a live phone camera into verified, object-tracked guidance—pointing users to the correct physical control.
about_excerpt: Field Assist lets Codex and a human expert turn a live phone camera into verified, object-tracked guidance—pointing users to the correct physical control. Like Comment Story Updates Connect a phone to the live support workspace with a one-time QR link. Phone-visible guidance points the operator toward the verified control. Codex asks the operator to confirm the identified physical device. The object-relative arrow remains associated with the target as the camera moves. Inspiration Earlier this week, before I discovered The WebMCP Challenge, I published experimental WebMCP support for GoFastr. When I saw the hackathon, my honest reaction was basically: “heck yeah—this is exactly what that package is for.” I wanted to test the browser-agent bridge against something much harder than a catalog or form demo. Remote support repeatedly fails at the last few inches: the operator is holding a phone, the expert says “press the button underneath,” and everyone is forced to translate vague language into physical action. Field Assist asks what happens when Codex, a human support representative, and the person holding the camera can share one live, structured workspace. Field Assist itself was built for this hackathon on top of that newly published GoFastr capability. What it does Field Assist creates a two-device support session. A support representative opens the desktop console and shares a one-time QR code. The operator scans it, grants rear-camera access, and selects a starter scenario or describes any problem in free form. The camera travels directly to the support browser over peer-to-peer WebRTC; the application server never records or relays the video. Codex joins through the authenticated support page’s WebMCP tools. It loads the application’s operating contract, reads the operator’s request, inspects the visible scene, and combines vision with product knowledge to form a hypothesis. When identity is uncertain, Codex asks the operator a bounded question on the phone. Once the device and its actionable control are separately verified, Codex can send a large phone-visible instruction and place an arrow at the control. The support representative can inspect, correct, compose, or remove the same shared guidance. OpenCV, Depth Anything V2, Canvas tracking, and short-lived phone orientation data help keep the arrow associated with the physical target as the camera moves. When geometry becomes unsafe, Field Assist suppresses the marker and asks for reacquisition instead of pretending it still knows. Why WebMCP Why is this a strong fit for WebMCP? Field Assist depends on live, authenticated browser state: a private camera session, changing scene geometry, operator answers, tracking confidence, and delivery receipts. WebMCP lets Codex use those application concepts directly instead of guessing at UI controls or receiving a giant screenshot-and-prompt dump. How does it create a better user experience? The operator keeps one hand on the phone and receives large, timely instructions plus spatial guidance where they are already looking. Codex and human support share the same backend-authoritative scene, conversation, question, and banner state, so the operator does not repeat context or translate ambiguous chat into physical action. What can people and agents do together that was difficult before? The person supplies intent, judgment, and physical confirmation. Codex contributes vision, product knowledge, structured questions, and rapid guidance. Together they can identify an unfamiliar device, confirm the correct object, locate a small control, guide the operator toward it, and withdraw the annotation if tracking becomes unsafe—all inside one live support session. How did I implement WebMCP? The authenticated support page exposes twenty-five tools generated by GoFastr through the standard document.modelContext.registerTool API. Read tools return versioned session and scene state. Mutating tools call the same authenticated Go handlers as the human controls and must include the current contextVersion. Landing and operator pages expose no support capabilities. How we built it Field Assist is one Go 1.27 service built on the released GoFastr v0.75.0 module. GoFastr provides the server-rendered application host, typed handlers, security middleware, WebSocket hub, lifecycle endpoints, structured logs, static plugin assets, and experimental WebMCP bridge. The authenticated support page declares twenty-five semantic tools for application context, scene inspection, object registration, room context, conversation, operator questions, banners, snapshots, and reversible spatial guidance. The mandatory get_app_info tool copies a versioned operating contract and the user’s current request into Codex context. Every state-changing tool must return that context version, which prevents an agent from acting against stale instructions. Browser-native WebRTC sends video directly from the phone to the support computer. GoFastr WebSockets carry only signaling and compact shared state. The support computer runs OpenCV ORB/RANSAC homography and PnP tracking alongside Depth Anything V2 Small through ONNX Runtime Web. A lightweight phone tracker and bounded DeviceOrientation samples bridge short visual gaps over a peer-to-peer data channel. Camera pixels, descriptors, depth maps, orientation samples, SDP, and ICE candidates are never stored by the application server. The interfaces are responsive and deliberately asymmetric: the phone prioritizes the live camera, large instructions, questions, answer acknowledgment, and chat; the desktop prioritizes the shared scene, support conversation, guidance controls, delivery state, and progressive diagnostics. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was not drawing an arrow—it was deciding when an arrow was trustworthy. Early versions anchored annotations to screen coordinates, confused a broad device with a tiny physical control, or kept displaying stale guidance after tracking loss. Reflective televisions and dark hardware exposed every weakness in monocular depth and feature matching. Another challenge was keeping three participants synchronized: the operator, human support, and Codex. Local optimistic UI caused banners and answers to disagree between screens, so the backend became authoritative for conversation, questions, banners, scene versions, and delivery receipts. Testing a two-device, hands-busy experience was also physically awkward. I repeatedly had to hold the phone in front of real hardware while Codex operated the support console. Those sessions forced the application contract to become explicit: inspect first, confirm uncertain identity, register the containing device before its control, send movement instructions to the phone banner, verify rendered delivery, and fail closed when tracking confidence drops. video_transcript_excerpt: Words fail when remote support asks, "Which button?" Field Assist lets an agent see, confirm, and point directly into the live view. A support session begins with a secure QR code. The operator scans it on their phone and shares the camera peer-to-peer without installing an app, creating an account, or streaming the video through the application server. Here, the operator needs help finding the power control on a PlayStation. Codex inspects the live scene through Web MCP and turns what it sees into a specific testable identification. Before acting on the physical world, the operator confirms the detected object. That human checkpoint prevents the assistant from confidently guiding someone toward the wrong device. Once confirmed, the support console starts visual tracking and spatial perception. OpenCV follows image features, depth, and anything estimate scene structure, and phone orientation data helps compensate as the camera moves. Codex uses its product knowledge and the live visual context to locate the likely power control. It then sends one clear instruction to the phone where it is impossible to miss while the operator is holding the camera. The arrow is not merely pinned to screen coordinates. Field Assist continually corrects it against the tracked object and scene geometry as the operator changes position. The support agent can verify the placement, recalibrate when confidence drops, and keep the instruction synchronized across both screens. >> The same interaction applies far beyond consumer electronics, equipment repair, device setup, field service, accessibility, independent living, remote care, warehouse picking, inspections, and safety training. Anywhere pointing is clearer than describing, remote expertise can become actionable. The stack combines codecs and web MCP with go faster, web RTC, open CV, depth anything, ONNX runtime web, and phone orientation, all in one web app. Field Assist turns remote expertise into guidance anchored to the real world.

live_observation.first_impression: A focused Field Assist landing page explains live spatial support and offers a secure-session start.
live_observation.after_state: A support console opened with an operator-camera pairing screen, QR/join link, conversation box, and current step Pair the operator.
